```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
inla_available <- bdlnm::check_inla()
```

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(bdlnm)
library(dlnm)
library(splines)
```

This vignette adapts the interaction-model tutorial developed by Marcos Quijal-Zamorano. It reproduces the age-specific temperature–mortality analysis using the higher-level functions provided by **bdlnm**, rather than implementing each step manually. The original tutorial is available at [Interaction model with Bayesian DLNMs](https://github.com/marcosqz/interaction_model_bdlnm/blob/main/Title.md).

The goal is to estimate the temperature–mortality association for two age groups (0–74 and 75+ years) in the city of London.

First, we have to convert the data from wide to long:

```{r}
london_age <- london |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mort_00_74, mort_75plus),
    names_to = "age",
    values_to = "mortality"
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    age = sub("^mort_", "", age),
    age = factor(age)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(age, date)
```

# Set DLNM parameters

We will start by building the crossbasis with the `dlnm` package. Because the long dataset contains one temperature series for each age group, we use the `group` argument to identify the two consecutive time series. This prevents lagged values from carrying over from one age group to the other.

We will use a natural spline with three knots for the exposure–response function, placed at the 10th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of daily mean temperature, and a natural spline for the lag–response function, with knots equally spaced on the log scale up to a maximum lag of 21 days:

```{r}
# Exposure-response and lag-response spline parameters
dlnm_var <- list(
  var_prc = c(10, 75, 90),
  var_fun = "ns",
  lag_fun = "ns",
  max_lag = 21,
  lagnk = 3
)


# Cross-basis parameters
argvar <- list(
  fun = dlnm_var$var_fun,
  knots = quantile(london$tmean, dlnm_var$var_prc / 100, na.rm = TRUE),
  Bound = range(london$tmean, na.rm = TRUE)
)

arglag <- list(
  fun = dlnm_var$lag_fun,
  knots = logknots(dlnm_var$max_lag, nk = dlnm_var$lagnk)
)

# Create the crossbasis for total mortality
cb_total <- crossbasis(
  london$tmean,
  lag = dlnm_var$max_lag,
  argvar,
  arglag
)

# Create the crossbasis for the age-specific model
cb <- crossbasis(
  london_age$tmean,
  lag = dlnm_var$max_lag,
  argvar,
  arglag,
  group = london_age$age
)
```

Let’s define the seasonality of the mortality time series using a natural spline with 8 degrees of freedom per year, which flexibly controls for long-term and seasonal trends in mortality:

```{r}
# Seasonality of mortality time series
n_years <- length(unique(london_age$date)) / 365.25
seas_total <- ns(london$date, df = round(8 * n_years))
seas <- ns(london_age$date, df = round(8 * n_years))
```

Finally, we also define the temperature values for which predictions will be generated. These correspond to an evenly spaced grid with a 0.1 °C step covering the full range of observed temperatures in the data:

```{r}
# Prediction values (equidistant points)
temp <- round(seq(min(london$tmean), max(london$tmean), by = 0.1), 1)
# Ensure it falls inside the range of temperatures after rounding:
temp <- temp[temp >= min(london$tmean) & temp <= max(london$tmean)]
```

# Estimate the common minimum mortality temperature

To make the age-specific associations directly comparable, both will be centered at the same temperature. This reference temperature will be set at the minimum mortality temperature (MMT) estimated from an overall model on the total mortality (`mort`):

```{r, eval = inla_available}
mod_total <- bdlnm(
  mort ~ cb_total + factor(dow) + seas_total,
  data = london,
  family = "poisson",
  sample.arg = list(n = 1000, seed = 1L)
)

cpred_total_uncentered <- bcrosspred(
  mod_total,
  exp_at = temp,
  cen = FALSE
)

mmt_total <- optimal_exposure(cpred_total_uncentered)
plot(mmt_total)
cen <- mmt_total$summary[["0.5quant"]]
```

# Fit the interaction model and posterior samples

We will fit a B-DLNM model in which the temperature–mortality association represented by the crossbasis interacts with age group:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
mod <- bdlnm(
  mortality ~ cb * age + factor(dow) * age + seas * age,
  data = london_age,
  family = "poisson",
  sample.arg = list(n = 1000, seed = 1L)
)
```

The `bdlnm()` function identifies the interaction term and expands it across all crossbasis coefficients. With treatment contrasts, `cb * age` produces standalone crossbasis coefficients for the reference age group and interaction coefficients describing how the association for the other age group differs:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
grep("cb", rownames(mod$coefficients), value = TRUE)
```

# Predict exposure-lag-response effects

We request age-specific predictions by including the fixed interaction in `combine_effects`, which combines the interaction coefficients for the second group with the standalone crossbasis coefficients. This returns one prediction for each age-group level, with both predictions evaluated over the same exposure and lag grids and relative to the same centering temperature:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
cpred <- bcrosspred(
  mod,
  combine_effects = ~ cb * age,
  exp_at = temp,
  cen = cen
)
```

A `bcrosspred` object is returned containing the estimated exposure–lag–response association for each age group:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
str(cpred, max.level = 1)
```

The `basis_interaction` attribute records information about the interaction:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
attr(cpred, "basis_interaction")
```

We can also obtain the predicted effects for the interaction specific coefficients, which represents the difference between the temperature–mortality associations for ages 75+ and 0–74. On the relative-risk scale, it can be interpreted as the ratio of their relative risks, centered at the common population MMT.

```{r}
cpred_interaction <- bcrosspred(
  mod,
  combine_effects = ~ cb:age,
  exp_at = temp,
  cen = cen
)
```

# Plot

## Exposure–lag–response associations

We can display the age-specific exposure–lag–response associations side by side:

```{r, eval = inla_available, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}
zlim <- range(
  cpred[["age[00_74]"]]$matRRfit.summary[, , "0.5quant"],
  cpred[["age[75plus]"]]$matRRfit.summary[, , "0.5quant"],
  na.rm = TRUE
)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(cpred, select = "age[00_74]", ptype = "3d", zlim = zlim, main = "Age 0–74")
plot(cpred, select = "age[75plus]", ptype = "3d", zlim = zlim, main = "Age 75+")
```

## Overall cumulative associations

The corresponding overall cumulative associations can be plotted for each age group and with the specific interaction effect:

```{r, eval = inla_available, fig.width = 14, fig.height = 5}
ylim <- range(
  cpred[["age[00_74]"]]$allRRfit,
  cpred[["age[75plus]"]]$allRRfit,
  cpred_interaction[["age[75plus]"]]$allRRfit,
  na.rm = TRUE
)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(cpred, select = "age[00_74]", ptype = "overall", ylim = ylim, main = "Age 0–74")
plot(cpred, select = "age[75plus]", ptype = "overall", ylim = ylim, main = "Age 75+")
plot(
  cpred_interaction,
  select = "age[75plus]",
  ptype = "overall",
  ylim = ylim,
  ylab = "Relative-risk ratio",
  main = "Age interaction: 75+ vs 0–74"
)
```
